sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: online with a university library login; also in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number 2235.3.35)
sources.note: Silent on stress. Phonological preliminaries p. 92: 'The tonal systems of Krahn are complex and consist of rising and falling as well as level tones' (tones numbered 1 highest to 4 lowest; nasalization is a word-level suprasegmental; clitics belong to the phonological word). Footnote 3: 'Gbaeson tone is described in Duitsman (1978)'. Data from Gbaeson and Gborbo dialects (both Western Krahn).

sources.citation: Bing, Janet Mueller. 1991. Color terms and lexical classes in Krahn/Wobé. Studies in African Linguistics 22(3): 277-296.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Silent on stress; footnote 2 (p. 278) only: 'Numbers refer to phonemic tones with 1 indicating the highest, 4 the lowest, and combinations indicating contour tone (see Bing [1993b] and Bearth & Link [1980])'. Gborbo dialect.

sources.citation: Bearth, Thomas & Christa Link. 1980. The tone puzzle of Wobé. Studies in African Linguistics 11(2): 147-207.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sister variety Wobé (Wè Northern, weno1238; Tao dialect), not Western Krahn: 14 contrasting tones on short monosyllables, syllable shape C1(C2)V1(V2)(V3); vowel length noted; no statement on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Duitsman, John, Jana Bertkau & James Laesch. 1975. A survey of Kru dialects. Studies in African Linguistics 6(1): 77-103.

sources.note: About Kru/Klao, with Krahn only as comparison; sec. 4.4 Tone: 'Phonetically, there are three level tones and, in most dialects, at least one rising and at least one falling tone. As in Krahn, there is an amazing amount of tonal interaction between syllables'. No mention of stress or accent.
